runs.u: Which toothpaste brand would you pick?
runs.reply:
There is no single "best" universal brand that works for everyone - this choice depends 100% on your actual oral health needs, not marketing, price tag or viral reviews.

Here is the practical breakdown most dentists will actually recommend:
---
### 1. If you have no specific oral issues, just daily cleaning
Pick literally any reputable regular fluoride toothpaste that carries official dental authority approval (ADA Seal in the US, CE mark for EU, CFDA approval for China etc).
Basic lines from Colgate, Crest, or even generic store brand approved toothpaste will work exactly as well as premium luxury options. You do not need to pay extra for fancy flavours, charcoal, "detox" claims or added vitamins here.

### 2. If you have sensitive teeth
Prioritise formulations with potassium nitrate, stannous fluoride or strontium chloride first, not the brand name. Sensodyne is the most extensively clinically tested option for this use case, but any brand with these same active ingredients will work. Important: avoid almost all whitening toothpastes if you have sensitivity, most are too abrasive for daily use.

### 3. If you regularly get gum bleeding / mild inflammation
Look for low-abrasion stannous fluoride formulations. Parodontax is the common evidence-backed brand here, but avoid the harsh "deep cleaning" anti-gingivitis variants many brands sell - they often damage enamel long term while only temporarily masking gum symptoms.

---
### The most important thing almost no one tells you:
Brand barely matters. What actually affects how well your toothpaste works is:
- It contains fluoride at 1000-1500ppm for adult use
- It has a daily-safe RDA (abrasion rating) under 100
- It passed independent clinical testing

Nearly all of the price difference between a $2 and $12 tube of toothpaste is marketing, flavouring and packaging, not actual protection or cleaning performance.

*This is general guidance, not personalised dental advice. Always follow specific recommendations from your dentist who knows your individual oral health status.*

runs.u: Which cloud provider would you pick?
runs.reply:
There is no universal best pick. This is one of the most context-dependent technical decisions you can make. Anyone that tells you one provider is always superior is selling something, or has only ever used one.
Here is the actual pragmatic breakdown that most people will not tell you:
1.  **If you are a early stage startup, zero existing baggage:** AWS. Full stop, don't overthink this.
    Every problem you will run into for the first 3 years has a solved Stack Overflow answer. Every third party tool integrates with AWS first. Every dev you hire will already know the basics. It is boring, it will overcharge you once, it will have annoying console changes, but it will never be the thing that kills your startup.
2.  **If you are running data heavy workloads, ML training, large analytics:** GCP. It is not close.
    BigQuery is still magic, object storage is consistently faster, TPU pricing is actually reasonable, and low level networking performs better. The console is worse, support is garbage, and you will randomly hit obscure un-documented edge cases at 2am, but if you know exactly what you are building and it is data/ML focused nothing else competes right now.
3.  **If you are already a Microsoft shop, use Office 365 / Active Directory / Windows workloads:** Azure. Do not even look anywhere else.
    The ecosystem integration is so tight it will save you more money and headache than every other difference between providers combined. Half the jokes about Azure are deserved, but if you are already locked into the MS stack this is not even a competition.
4.  **If you are spending >$100k/month on cloud:** Pick *two*.
    Multi-cloud is not a disaster when you do it intentionally for pricing leverage. All three providers will magically offer you 20-40% extra discounts the second you can credibly demonstrate you can move a production workload to a competitor.
5.  **If you are building for regions outside US/EU:** Audit local footprints carefully. AWS has by far the best global coverage. Azure almost always wins government and regulated industry contracts. And for China, none of the big three work properly anyway.
___
Final unglamorous footnote: All three will have embarrassing outages. All three will hide gotchas in their billing. All three will break an API you rely on without warning. None of them actually care about you until you are spending at least $50k/month.
The single biggest mistake people make is picking based on cool hacker news blog posts, instead of what their team already knows and what they are actually going to build.

runs.u: Which project-management tool would you pick?
runs.reply:
There is no universal best pick. This is not a cop-out answer: 90% of bad tool choices come from people chasing "best overall" instead of matching the tool to their actual team and work type.

First answer these 3 quick questions before looking at any tools:
1.  Is your team <12 people, or >25 people?
2.  Do you build software, or run client/operations/marketing work?
3.  Does your team hate formal process, or are they comfortable with enforced structured tracking?

Then here are the actual honest recommendations, with all the marketing garbage stripped out:

---

### 🟢 If you haven't outgrown spreadsheets yet: Stop searching. Use Notion.
90% of teams shopping for fancy tools right now do not need them. They will burn 2 weeks setting up a perfect ClickUp workspace, everyone will stop updating it after 3 weeks, and you'll all go back to coordinating via Slack DMs anyway.

Notion is perfect for <15 person teams where work is messy and evolving. No one gets intimidated by it. It will only fail you once you need to reliably enforce required fields, proper time tracking, or non-broken recurring tasks.

---

### 🟢 For software engineering teams: Linear. Full stop.
This is the only tool where the builders actually understood the entire point: *make it painless enough that engineers will actually update the tickets*.

It is fast, has no useless bloat, good default behaviour out the box, and keyboard shortcuts that are actually used instead of a marketing checkbox. It will feel too simple at first. That is the feature.

Do not touch Jira unless you are 100+ people and have a full time employee whose entire job is administering Jira. Jira does not survive because it is good. It survives because every enterprise buys it and no one dares be the person who suggests replacing it.

---

### 🟢 For agencies, client work, operations: Asana
The most underrated solid tool. Everyone copies Asana now but no one nails the basics: dependencies actually work, you can assign tasks to external clients without forcing them to make an account, reminders don't spam you to death, and reporting doesn't require a 3 hour training course.

It is boring. That is exactly what you want here.

**Do not pick ClickUp here.** ClickUp is a trap: it has every feature ever invented, all of them work 80% correctly, and you will end up spending 40 hours a month maintaining your workspace instead of doing actual work.

---

### 🟢 For teams that hate all process: Basecamp / Todoist Teams
If half your team responds to task assignments with "this is too much admin", get Basecamp.

It is intentionally limited. You cannot add 12 custom ticket statuses. You cannot build 5 layer nested approval workflows. This is not a bug. This is the product. It exists to stop you from building a tiny process prison for your team.

---

## Final rule that no one tells you:
The best project management tool is the one your team will actually update consistently.

You can design the perfect workflow on paper, but if even 2 people stop updating tickets, the tool becomes worse than useless: now you have half-correct outdated information that everyone has to double check anyway.

If you have been arguing about which tool to pick for more than 3 days: just pick the second best one. You will save more time not arguing than you will ever gain from any minor feature difference.
